overview:
Sometime in the twelfth or thirteenth century, groups of Nahuatl-speaking migrants moved into the Basin of Mexico, a high valley of shallow lakes ringed by volcanoes. Their own histories, recorded generations later, told of a departure from a homeland called Aztlan and of the god Huitzilopochtli instructing them to drop the name Azteca and call themselves Mexica. They arrived late and poor, squatting on marginal land and serving as mercenaries for established city-states. By tradition they founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco in 1325, and the earliest excavated phase of its Templo Mayor dates to roughly that period. For a century they were tributaries of the Tepanec city of Azcapotzalco. That changed in 1428, when Tenochtitlan under Itzcoatl joined with Texcoco and Tlacopan to destroy Tepanec power and split the spoils — the Triple Alliance, which is what historians usually mean when they say "Aztec Empire."

What followed was less a unified state than a tribute machine. Successive rulers — Motecuhzoma I, Axayacatl, Ahuitzotl, Motecuhzoma II — pushed campaigns outward until dozens of subject provinces were sending cotton, cacao, feathers, jade and maize into the capital, while mostly keeping their own lords and gods. Tenochtitlan itself grew into one of the largest cities on earth, plausibly holding 200,000 people or more, fed by chinampa plots raised from the lakebed and linked to the shore by causeways and an aqueduct. At its center the Templo Mayor was rebuilt seven times, each enlargement roughly matching a new reign, carrying twin shrines to the rain god Tlaloc and to Huitzilopochtli. Human sacrifice was woven into that religious and political order, and its scale remains one of the most argued-over questions in the field, partly because the Spaniards who described it had every reason to exaggerate.

The collapse came fast and was not simply Spanish. Hernán Cortés landed in 1519 and reached Tenochtitlan by exploiting the resentments the tribute system had created, above all among the Tlaxcalans, who had never been conquered and who supplied the great majority of the fighters. Smallpox, arriving in 1520, killed a large share of the population including the ruler Cuitlahuac. The siege ran from May to August of 1521 and ended with the capture of Cuauhtemoc and the ruin of the island city, on which Mexico City was then built. Nahua people, language and institutions did not vanish with it; much of what is known about the Mexica was written down afterward by their own descendants, in Nahuatl, under colonial rule.
significance: The fall of Tenochtitlan is one of the hinges of world history: it opened mainland America to European colonization, funneled silver from Mexican mines into a genuinely global economy, and produced through conquest and catastrophe the mestizo society that became Mexico. It also gave Europe a lasting and distorted image of a "civilization" it had just destroyed, and gave later generations of Mexicans a founding symbol — the eagle on the cactus, still on the national flag. Beyond that, the Mexica remain one of the very few large pre-industrial states whose workings can be studied from documents written by the conquered themselves, which makes them a permanent test case for how historians read sources produced under domination.
coverage: This dataset currently holds no events at all beneath the story, so nothing here is drawn from it — the account above comes from reference works and from the Mexican national institute's account of the Templo Mayor excavations. The deeper problem is the record itself: almost no pre-conquest books survive, so Mexica history before 1519 reaches us through colonial-era manuscripts like the Florentine Codex, compiled decades later by Nahua authors working under Franciscan supervision, and through Spanish accounts written by men justifying what they had done. Dates before about 1400, including the 1325 founding, are traditional rather than firmly documented, and figures for sacrifice, population and army sizes are contested by an order of magnitude. The dataset's 1523 end date is later than the 1521 siege and is not explained here.
